title: You DON’T Descend From All Your Ancestors
description:
This video explains the difference between genetic and genealogical descent, showing why most of our genetic ancestry is lost over a short number of generations.  For further information, check out David Reich’s book, Who We Are and How We Got Here: https://www.amazon.com/Who-Are-How-Got-Here/dp/110187032X/

Download the soundtrack to this video here: https://ko-fi.com/marcusgallo9000

Music made with FL Studio
Art made with Asesprite 
Animations made with After Effects

segments.text: You don’t descend genetically from all your ancestors.
The human genome is made
up of more than 3 billion base pairs, the nucleic acids that bind to one another to form the double
helix structure of DNA. There are only four types of base pairs: adenine always pairs with thymine
and cytosine always pairs with guanine.
Now, you might imagine that 3 billion base pairs is a very large number. And you’d be right. But
remember that the number of your ancestors doubles every generation. We only need to go back 32
generations, to roughly 1200 AD, before each of us has over 4 billion 30th-great-grandparents.
If we were to descend equally from all of our ancestors, we would reach a hard limit around
this time. With more ancestors than units of DNA, we simply could not descend from everyone.
Having said this, one might imagine that it is
irrelevant how many theoretical ancestors a person had 32 generations ago. Due to cousin marriage,
many of the same people appear in different places in our family tree, so we would have far fewer
actual ancestors than base pairs of DNA. In fact, it would not be possible to have 4 billion
ancestors living in 1200 AD -- we now estimate that only 450 million people lived on the planet
at that time. Even if a person living today managed to be descended from all of them, this is
a far smaller number than the limit of 3 billion base pairs. We could say the same thing about
earlier human populations: no matter how far we go back in time, there would be fewer people living
on the planet than there are base pairs in our genomes. Those individual ancestors would appear
over and over again in our ancestry, distributed over many different parts of our family trees.
Therefore, we should still be able to get genetic material from all of those ancestors.
But this is not how human descent
works. We do not descend equally from all of our ancestors, as David Reich explains in his book,
Who We Are and How We Got Here.
Each of us gets 23 chromosomes from our fathers and 23 from our mothers, arranged in pairs.
Two chromosomes determine sex. Men
receive an X chromosome from their mothers, but a Y chromosome from their fathers. Because of this,
we can trace a man’s direct paternal ancestor (his father’s father’s father, going back millennia),
by looking at his Y chromosome.
It’s impossible to use this method to trace a woman’s direct maternal ancestor (her mother’s
mother’s mother, going back millennia), because women receive X chromosomes from both parents.
However, we only receive mitochondrial DNA from our mothers. We can therefore trace
anyone’s direct maternal ancestor by looking at mitochondrial DNA.
As a result,
each of us is born with 47 distinct pieces of DNA: 23 chromosomes from each parent, and 1 complete
set of mitochondrial DNA from our mothers.
But we do not transmit those chromosomes fully intact to the next generation. Instead,
during meiosis, the pairs of chromosomes are interspliced. When a man forms a sperm, he creates
a set of 23 chromosomes that has an average of 26 splices. Any chromosome in a typical sperm
will therefore have about half of its DNA from the man’s father and half from the man’s mother. When
a woman forms an egg, she creates an average of 45 splices. So the chromosomes in eggs will be split
so that roughly one third comes from one of her parents and two-thirds come from the other parent.
Unlike a man’s intact Y chromosome, the crossover of genes affects all of a woman’s chromosomes,
including her X chromosomes, so that the X chromosomes she passes to her children mix the
DNA from both of her own parents’ X chromosomes.
In every generation, these splits take place at different spots on the genome, and there
are different numbers of splits that form each time. But on average, every generation adds 71
more splices than the generation before. Knowing this allows genetic researchers to estimate the
familial relatedness of two people by looking at their genomes: if they share identical sections
of DNA, the longer those sections are, the closer in time they are related. This is because there
have been fewer random splicing events that have disrupted the shared stretches of DNA.
This also creates a fascinating genetic lottery:
as generations advance, some ancestors will contribute disproportionately to a descendant’s
DNA, and some will contribute nothing at all.
Why? Each generation, the number of DNA stretches only grows by 71 while the number of ancestors
doubles. In other words, the units of genetic descent increase arithmetically, but the units of
genealogical descent increase exponentially.
So, for example, 3 generations back, you have 8 great-grandparents, whose genetic contribution
will be divided into 260 pieces. On average, each will contribute about 5 or 6 chromosomes’ worth of
DNA in 32 large stretches.
Nine generations back, say around the year 1800, you have 512 ancestors, whose genetic contribution
will be divided into 686 pieces. Although you still have more genetic slots than you
have ancestors, some of these ancestors will have passed none of their genes on to you,
and some will have multiple stretches of DNA that they gave to you completely
intact. At this point, only 72 percent of these 7th-great-grandparents will give you some of your
genetics.
It only takes a short time for the number of your genealogical ancestors to dwarf the number
of your genetic ancestors. Fifteen generations back, say around the year 1650, when the first
English colonies began to be founded in North America, you have 32,768 genealogical ancestors,
but only 1,112 genetic ancestors. Over less than 400 years, 97 percent of your ancestors contribute
nothing to your genetics.
The same is true in the reverse direction. If you have living descendants in 400 years,
you have only a 3 percent chance of contributing anything at all to their genome, unless you are
lucky enough to be s omeone’s direct maternal or paternal ancestor. Soon, any contributions you
do make will appear in slivers of DNA so tiny that it becomes difficult to distinguish whether you or
some other ancestor made the contribution.
Within a very short time, we descend from an anonymous stream of humanity, we are
individually shaped by a few recent ancestral generations, we strongly shape a few generations
of our descendants, and then our contribution passes into an anonymous stream of humanity.
With the aid of some speculation, an example
from a royal family can help illustrate this.
The current King of the United Kingdom is Charles III. At the bottom of the screen, his
father’s contribution to his DNA is highlighted in purple and his mother’s is highlighted in orange.
Charles’s mother was Elizabeth II,
who was Queen for 70 years, from 1952 to 2022. Charles inherited half of his genome from her,
including his X chromosome and his mitochondrial DNA. This contribution to Charles’s DNA remains
highlighted in orange.
Her father was George VI, King during World War II. Already at this stage of descent,
the randomness of meiosis begins to play a role: grandparents do not contribute equally to their
grandchildren. In our hypothetical scenario, we might imagine that George contributed slightly
more than half of the genes that Elizabeth passed on to Charles. This contribution remains
highlighted at the bottom of the screen.
George’s father (Charles’s great-grandfather) was George V, King during World War I. In our
scenario, George V contributed a heavy proportion of the genes that his son eventually passes on to
Charles. Note that despite his genetic closeness to Charles, George V’s DNA makes no contribution
at all to Chromosome 17.
George V’s father was Edward VII, who was heir apparent for 60 years and King for 9. At this
stage, each ancestor should account for 6.25% of their great-great-grandchildren’s genes. In our
scenario, Edward instead contributed 10.33%.
His mother (Charles’s 3rd-great-grandmother) was Queen Victoria, who ruled England for most of the
19th century and whose 9 children intermarried with the various royal houses of Europe and thus
fought on both sides of World War I.
Her father was Prince Edward of Kent and Strathearn, who had an unimpressive
military career that ended prematurely after he was stripped of command of the outpost of
Gibraltar following a mutiny. He theoretically remained Governor of Gibraltar but was forbidden
to travel there again. Because Edward was Charles’s 4th-great-grandfather,
one of 64 ancestors contributing to 473 genetic slots, it is almost certain that he
passed on genes to Charles. In our scenario, he contributed an outsized 5.3% of Charles’s genome.
Edward’s mother was Charlotte, a
German who married George III and became the Queen of Great Britain during the American Revolution.
In reality, she very likely contributed to King Charles’s genetics, although on average,
ancestors of her generation contributed less than a percent each. In our scenario, she contributed
2.6% of Charles’s genome.
Charlotte’s father, Charles Louis Frederick, was three months old when his own father died. He
never inherited the duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz and lived in a small castle, where he enjoyed
playing the transverse flute. There is a 91% chance that he contributed to King Charles’s
genetics.
Adolphus Frederick II was himself born posthumously and ruled over the small
province of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. There is a 72% chance that he contributed to King Charles’s
genetics. By this point, 9 generations deep into a family tree, the average ancestor contributes a
single snippet of DNA to their descendant. In our scenario, Duke Adolphus contributed a hefty 0.66%
of Charles’s genome.
The Duke’s father, Adolphus Frederick I, reigned as Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin throughout the
first half of the 1600s, except for a brief time when Catholics under von Wallenstein seized the
province during the Thirty Years’ War. There is a 50% chance that he contributed something to King
Charles’s genetics.
His mother Sophia had married the Duke of Mecklenburg, who later split the duchy in half
for his two sons. There is a 32% chance that she contributed anything to King Charles’s genetics.
Sophia’s mother Christine was one
of ten children of the Landgrave of Hesse and was almost married to the King of Sweden, but instead
married the Duke of Holstein-Gottorp. There is a 19% chance that she contributed anything to
King Charles’s genetics. In our scenario, she contributed exactly the same stretches of DNA
to Charles that her daughter did, making their genetic contributions to him indistinguishable.
Christine’s mother, also
named Christine, was married to Philip of Hesse, who felt disgusted by her and openly practiced
a bigamous marriage with another woman. There is an 11% chance that she contributed anything
to King Charles’s genetics. In our scenario, we have arrived at a single tiny snippet of DNA
shared between Christine and her descendant Charles, amounting to 0.05% of his genome.
Christine’s mother Barbara was married
to the Duke of Saxony in front of more than 6,000 Polish and German nobles. There is a 6% chance
that she contributed anything to King Charles’s genetics. In our scenario, her contribution to
Charles mirrored that of her daughter Christine.
Barbara’s father Casimir IV Jagiellon ruled Lithuania and Poland from the 1440s until 1492,
when that territory stretched from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. There is only a 3% chance that
he contributed anything to King Charles’s genetics. In our hypothetical scenario,
he is the first genealogical ancestor in this line of descent to contribute nothing
to King Charles’s genome. All of Casimir’s myriad ancestors would also contribute nothing at all to
Charles’s genetics.
As Charles’s case illustrates, had our genealogical ancestors not existed,
we would not exist, but their genetic contributions to us disappear with time,
much like our memories of them.
The same will become true for us and our own genetic contributions to our future descendants.
In a few short centuries, those descendants will resemble us only insofar as we are all made up
of the DNA of our ancient forebears, long since shattered into a cacophony of tiny fragments.
